newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Engen says H2 net income may be lower.
newsitem.headline: Engen says H2 net income may be lower.

text.p: South African oil company, Engen Ltd, said on Monday that net income in the second half of the 1996/97 year may be lower than in the first half, bar a possible increase in regulated marketing margins.

Releasing group results for the six months to February 28, chief executive officer Rob Angel said that although operating income was likely to match the period under review, the bottomline could come under pressure from lower oil prices.

"Should current rand crude and product prices continue through to the 1997 financial year end, an inventory loss similar in size to the first half gain would be reported for the second half of the 1997 financial year," Angel told reporters.
"In these circumstances...the company's net income for the second half of the financial year would be lower than that reported for the first half."

Engen reported an inventory profit of 38 million rand in the first six months, helped by higher crude oil prices in the last quarter of 1996. Prices have fallen sharply since the start of the year to around $18 from near $24 late in 1996, Angel said.
At the same time the rand has strengthened, pushing down rand prices even further.

Overall in the review period Engen's bottomline earnings rose 21.6 percent to 107.0 cents a share from 88 cents last time -- slightly ahead of a Reuters consensus forecast earnings of 103.2 cents. The dividend was held steady at 36.0 cents a share.

Angel said that isolated operational hitches continued in the period at Engen's Durban-based refinery, where major problems in 1995 pummelled earnings, with crude oil throughput down by 2.6 percent and white oil yields slightly lower.
"We have seen a good thrust of improved reliability...But this was impacted upon by a couple of incidents during the period, one in September and one in February," Angel said.

Another factor which would continue to weigh on Engen, along with the rest of the South African oil industry, was a lack of action from government on deregulating the fuel market and in raising the wholesale fuel margin, Angel said.
"I think the impression we are getting is of a status quo. If the market is deregulated it will fly in the face of a few government imperatives, such as jobs," he said.
Fears have been raised that a move to deregulation and a move to self-service at gasoline outlets could lead to heavy job losses.

The industry applied to the minerals and energy affairs ministry in April 1996 for a three cents per litre margin rise after its return on marketing assets in 1995 fell to 8.7 percent versus a 15 percent target as specified in current regulations. The ministry has not responded to the request.
